title: Choosing a move when an opponent chooses next
intro: A route-finding problem lets you choose every step. In a game, your opponent chooses some of the next steps. We will build a rule that accounts for both players, then see when part of a game tree can be skipped.

sections.title: 1. Give every outcome the same point of view
text: Suppose two players take turns, and a larger final score is better for the first player. Call that player MAX. Call the opponent MIN because the opponent prefers a smaller score for MAX.
A leaf is a finished outcome at the end of a branch. Its utility is the score assigned to that outcome. Keep every score from MAX’s point of view, including scores below a MIN turn.

At a MAX turn, select the largest available child value. At a MIN turn, select the smallest. This rule assumes the opponent chooses the move best for them in this deterministic, two-player, zero-sum setting.
sections.example: If MAX can finish at scores 2 or 7, MAX chooses 7. If MIN chooses between those same scores, MIN chooses 2. We keep the score scale fixed rather than changing its sign at each turn.
sections.question: A MIN node has leaf scores 6,1,4. What value should it pass to its parent? Why?
sections.answer: It passes 1. MIN can force the smallest score for MAX by choosing that child.

sections.title: 2. Work upward from the leaves
text: Now place a MAX node at the root. It has two children L and R. Each child is a MIN node. L has leaf scores 3 and 5. R has leaf scores 2 and 9.
First solve each decision where the outcomes are already known. L passes up min(3,5)=3. R passes up min(2,9)=2. The root then chooses max(3,2)=3.

This repeated minimum-or-maximum calculation is minimax. The value 3 means MAX can secure that score under the stated tree and optimal play. MAX should choose L even though R contains the largest individual leaf, 9. MIN would prevent MAX from receiving that leaf.

sections.title: 3. Keep the best choice already available
text: Search the tree left to right. Once L returns 3, MAX already has an option worth 3. A new branch matters only if it can beat that option.
The bound called alpha records the best lower bound MAX can secure along the current search path. At this root, alpha becomes 3.
Begin examining R. Its first leaf is 2. Because R is a MIN node, finding more children can keep its value at 2 or reduce it. The value of R can never rise above 2 after this observation.
sections.example: Compare the two facts: MAX can already get 3 from L. R can give at most 2. The second leaf of R cannot change which root move is best.
sections.question: If the unseen leaf under R were 100 instead of 9, could R beat L? Explain.
sections.answer: No. R would still choose min(2,100)=2. If the unseen leaf were smaller than 2, R would become even worse for MAX.

sections.title: 4. Use the bounds to stop a branch
text: The bound called beta records the best upper bound MIN can enforce along the current path. After R sees leaf 2, its beta is 2. The root’s alpha is 3.
When alpha≥beta, the current branch cannot improve the relevant earlier decision. Stop exploring that branch. This is alpha–beta pruning. Pruning saves work while preserving the root’s minimax value.
A partially explored node may give a bound rather than its exact value. Here we know R is at most 2. That is enough to choose L, even if the skipped leaf could make R smaller.

What we knowBound
MAX’s completed option LAt least 3

DecisionSkip R’s remaining leaf

sections.title: 5. Order changes the work, not the game value
text: Swap the order of R’s leaves, so it shows 9 before 2. After seeing 9, MIN’s current upper bound is 9. MAX’s existing option is still 3.
The inequality 3≥9 is false. R might still beat L, so we must inspect its second leaf. That leaf is 2, and R finally returns 2. MAX still chooses L with value 3.

Good move ordering often allows earlier cutoffs. It does not change the minimax result of a fully evaluated finite tree. For each cutoff, state both bounds and name the earlier decision that makes the remaining work unnecessary.
sections.example: Left-to-right examination of leaves 2,9 permits a cutoff after 2. Examination of 9,2 needs both. The opponent has the same two options in either order.

sections.title: 6. Check the full idea on a new tree
text: Try a MAX root whose MIN children have leaves (4,7) and (6,2). First compute the result without pruning. Then trace left-to-right alpha–beta.

The first child returns 4, setting alpha to 4. The second child first sees 6, so no cutoff follows yet. It must inspect 2 and returns 2. The root value is 4. This example needs every leaf in that order.
sections.example: Now put 2 first under the second child. It immediately gives beta=2≤alpha=4, so the remaining 6 can be skipped.
sections.question: What must you show when claiming that a leaf can be skipped?
sections.answer: Identify the available alternative, the current lower and upper bounds, and why no unseen child in this branch can improve the earlier choice.

remember: MAX chooses a larger utility. MIN chooses a smaller one.
Solve a finite tree upward from its leaves.
Alpha and beta bound choices along the current path.
A cutoff needs a reason based on bounds, not a guess about the hidden leaves.
review: On another day, ask your tutor for a different game tree. Compute its value before tracing pruning. Change the child order and compare the leaves inspected.
